case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. [Persona]

Case:
A 72-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic aortic valve implanted 6 years prior to presentation was evaluated for fevers, malaise, and weight loss. Five months prior, she developed fevers and chills while visiting the island of Elba, where she consumed raw milk products. Two weeks after initial improvement, she developed intermittent night sweats, fevers up to 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), fatigue, and weight loss of 10 kg (22.05 lb). At presentation, her temperature was 37.8 °C (100 °F); heart rate, 71 beats/min; and blood pressure, 126/80 mm Hg. Physical examination was normal except for a grade 2 cardiac systolic ejection murmur. Laboratory findings revealed a normal complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and transaminase level. C-reactive protein level was 13 mg/L (reference, <5 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 50 mm/h (reference, <20 mm/h). Rheumatoid factor level was 68 U/mL (reference, <14 U/mL). Results ofTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination and HIV testing were negative. Two sets of blood cultures showed no growth after 7 days. Findings of chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans were normal. An initial electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min and first-degree atrioventricular block. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TEE) revealed a normally functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve without vegetations. A TEE (Figure 1) showed normal valvular function and a thickened aortic root. You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

[Case context]
A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

Agreed, the gene panel is definitive. Adding neuroacanthocytosis to the differential is astute given the chorea and abnormal RBCs; the panel should include genes like VPS13A and XK to cover that spectrum.

[AI assistant's reply]
Perfect. Expanding the panel to include VPS13A and XK for neuroacanthocytosis syndromes is an excellent and comprehensive plan, given the full triad of chorea, myopathy, and acanthocytes.

[Case context]
A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

[AI assistant's reply]
Perfect. Coordinating these steps ensures a seamless transition from diagnosis to definitive management, which is crucial for a lesion with this concerning progression. Please keep me updated on the biopsy results.

case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred.
